subject: Cooking
title: Sauerkraut: Germany's Probiotic Powerhouse
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Sauerkraut: Germany's Probiotic Powerhouse.

hook.text: Sauerkraut is just cabbage and salt. No vinegar, no cooking. Bacteria do everything else.

buildup.text: Salt draws water from cabbage via osmosis, creating a brine. Lactobacillus bacteria begin converting sugars to acid.

discovery.text: Within days, the pH drops below 4.6 — creating an environment where only beneficial bacteria survive.

twist.text: Captain James Cook brought sauerkraut barrels on voyages — its vitamin C prevented scurvy at sea.

climax.text: Unpasteurized sauerkraut contains more probiotics per serving than most commercial supplements.

punchline.text: Two ingredients. Zero cooking. Maximum nutrition.

quiz.question: What are the only two ingredients in traditional sauerkraut?

details.summary: Sauerkraut is cabbage fermented in salt by naturally occurring Lactobacillus bacteria. The salt draws out water, creates brine, and selects for beneficial bacteria that produce lactic acid. This ancient preservation method yields a tangy, crunchy food rich in vitamins C and K.
details.whyItMatters: Sauerkraut is one of the simplest fermented foods to make — just cabbage and salt. It demonstrates how fermentation preserves food while creating new flavors and boosting nutritional value.
takeaways: Only cabbage and salt are needed — bacteria come from the cabbage
Lactic acid bacteria produce the sour flavor and preserve the food
Properly fermented sauerkraut stays preserved for months

faq.question: How much salt does sauerkraut need?
faq.answer: The standard ratio is 2 to 3 percent salt by weight of cabbage. Too little salt allows harmful bacteria to compete. Too much salt inhibits the desired lactic acid bacteria. About one tablespoon of salt per pound of cabbage is the reliable guideline.

faq.question: Is store-bought sauerkraut as healthy as homemade?
faq.answer: Most store-bought sauerkraut is pasteurized, which kills the beneficial bacteria. Look for refrigerated, unpasteurized varieties labeled with live cultures. Canned sauerkraut has been heat-treated and contains no living probiotics, though it retains fiber and some vitamins.
